claims.text: The initial material is an as-cast face-centered-cubic high-entropy alloy.
Ab initio-guided metastability engineering can introduce controlled lattice distortions in high-entropy alloys.
Ab initio-guided metastability engineering can introduce controlled atomic-scale segregation in high-entropy alloys.
Controlled lattice distortions reduce the alloy's stacking-fault energy.
Controlled atomic-scale segregation reduces the alloy's stacking-fault energy.
The reduction in stacking-fault energy improves strength and ductility.
Controlled lattice distortions and atomic-scale segregation enhance fracture resistance.
The strategy will increase strength by 20% relative to current high-entropy alloys with optimal property combinations.
The strategy will increase ductility by 30% relative to current high-entropy alloys with optimal property combinations.
The strategy will increase Young's modulus by 10% relative to current high-entropy alloys with optimal property combinations.
The strategy will increase fracture resistance by 25% relative to current high-entropy alloys with optimal property combinations.
The proposed property improvements apply under structural-service temperatures up to 500°C.
The proposed property improvements apply under stresses up to 1000 MPa.
The strategy is effective only within a specific, but unquantified, range of lattice distortion and atomic-scale segregation.
The strategy will not be applicable when segregation is excessive.
The strategy will not be applicable when precipitates form.
The relationship among lattice distortion, atomic-scale segregation, and mechanical properties is not fully understood.
Failure to achieve minimum improvements of 15% in strength, 20% in ductility, 5% in Young's modulus, and 15% in fracture resistance is specified as falsifying the hypothesis.
